newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council threatens new sanctions against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council threatens new sanctions against Iraq.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Saturday adopted a resolution threatening new sanctions against Iraq if it does not permit free inspections by international arms experts.

An agreement on the resolution was forged in Denver between President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin during the Group of Seven summit among industrial nations. Russia earlier had threatened to veto a tougher U.S.-British draft that wanted to impose travel sanctions immediately on officials blocking three inspections during the last month.

The vote was a unanimous 15-0 on the resolution that expresses the council's "firm intention to impose additional measures" on Iraqi officials responsible for barring the U.N. arms inspectors from three sites earlier this month. Baghdad argued it had the right to restrict access to sensitive sites that affect national security.

The resolution also suspends until Oct. 30 regular council reviews, usually held every 60 days, on the current stringent trade sanctions imposed on Iraq since it invaded Kuwait in August 1990. A report on Oct. 11 by the inspectors could trigger movement on new sanctions.
A condition for lifting oil exports is certification by the U.N. Special Commission, known as UNSCOM, that Iraq had rid itself of weapons of mass destruction and related items.

Both the United States and Russia said they were satisfied with the compromise -- the United States because the resolution affirmed the principle of new sanctions. Russia was pleased because sanctions were not imposed immediately and another resolution would be needed to enact any new measures, its U.N. envoy said.
